A non-ambient *variable declaration* introduces a new variable which is in fact
a named storage location. A declared variable must be assigned an initial value
before the first usage. The initial value is assigned either as a part of the
declaration or in various forms via initialization.

The syntax of *variable declarations* is presented below:

.. code-block:: abnf

    variableDeclarations:
        'let' variableDeclarationList
        ;

    variableDeclarationList:
        variableDeclaration (',' variableDeclaration)*
        ;

    variableDeclaration:
        identifier ':' type initializer?
        | identifier initializer
        ;

    initializer:
        '=' expression
        ;

When a variable is introduced by a variable declaration, type ``T`` of the
variable is determined as follows:

-  ``T`` is the type specified in a type annotation (if any) of the declaration.

   - If the declaration also has an initializer, then the initializer expression
     type must be assignable to ``T`` (see :ref:`Assignability with Initializer`).

-  If no type annotation is available, then ``T`` is inferred from the
   initializer expression (see :ref:`Type Inference from Initializer`).

An ambient variable declaration (see 
:ref:`Ambient Constant or Variable Declarations`) must have *type*
but no *initializer*. Otherwise, a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.

================

.. meta:

Integer literals represent numbers that have neither a decimal point nor
an exponential part. Integer literals can be written with radices 16
(hexadecimal), 10 (decimal), 8 (octal), and 2 (binary) as follows:

.. index::
   integer
   literal
   hexadecimal
   decimal
   octal
   binary
   radix

.. code-block:: abnf

    IntegerLiteral:
      DecimalIntegerLiteral
      | HexIntegerLiteral
      | OctalIntegerLiteral
      | BinaryIntegerLiteral
      ;

    DecimalIntegerLiteral:
      '0'
      | DecimalDigitNotZero ('_'? DecimalDigit)*
      ;

    DecimalDigit:
      [0-9]
      ;

    DecimalDigitNotZero:
      [1-9]
      ;

    HexIntegerLiteral:
      '0' [xX]  ( HexDigit
      | HexDigit (HexDigit | '_')* HexDigit
      )
      ;

    HexDigit:
      [0-9a-fA-F]
      ;

    OctalIntegerLiteral:
      '0' [oO] ( OctalDigit
      | OctalDigit (OctalDigit | '_')* OctalDigit )
      ;

    OctalDigit:
      [0-7]
      ;

    BinaryIntegerLiteral:
      '0' [bB] ( BinaryDigit
      | BinaryDigit (BinaryDigit | '_')* BinaryDigit )
      ;

    BinaryDigit:
      [0-1]
      ;

Integral literals with different radices are represented by the examples below:

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    153 // decimal literal
    1_153 // decimal literal
    0xBAD3 // hex literal
    0xBAD_3 // hex literal
    0o777 // octal literal
    0b101 // binary literal

The underscore character ``'_'`` between successive
digits can be used to improve readability.
Underscore characters in such positions do not change the values of literals.
However, the underscore character must be neither the very first nor the very
last symbol of an integer literal.

A numeric value ``v`` is converted to ``U``:sub:`i` of union type

      to the value type.

   required.

.. _Specifics of Constant Expressions Evaluation:

Specifics of Constant Expressions Evaluation
============================================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Done

If a constant expression contains an unary or a binary operator applied
to numeric operands, the operator is evaluated as follows:

- If any of operands are of type ``double`` or the operator is
  *exponentiation operator*, other operands are converted to type ``double``
  before operator evaluation and the result type is ``double``;

- If any of operands are of type ``float``, other operands are converted
  to type ``float`` before operator evaluation and the result type is
  ``float``; or

- Otherwise, all operands are converted to *some big integer type* that allows
  handling arbitrary-precision integers (like ``bigint`` type) or integers
  larger than the maximum value of type ``long``.

If a constant expression consists of a single integer literal or
a constant of an integer type, it is also converted to the same big integer type.

:ref:`Type Inference for Constant Expressions` is always used to infer the
type of constant expression. In other words, *big integer type* is an
internal compiler type and values of this type cannot occur during execution.

In case of mixed constant expression, each numeric subexpression is evaluated
as described above:

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    const c = 3

    c > 1 && c*2 < 8 // numeric subexpressions: (c > 1) and (c*2 < 8)

.. _Constant Expressions:

Constant Expressions
********************

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Done

*Constant expressions* are expressions with values that can be evaluated at
compile time. If the evaluation *completes abruptly*, then a
:index:`compile-time error` occurs.

The syntax of *constant expression* is presented below:

.. code-block:: abnf

    constantExpression:
        expression
        ;

A *constant expression* can be either of a value type (see
:ref:`Value Types`) or of type ``string``, while being composed only of the
following:

-  Literals of a predefined value types, and literals of type ``string`` (see
   :ref:`Literals`);

-  Simple names that refer to constants declared in a surrounding block,
   function, method, or lambda body, if the initializer of the referenced
   constant declaration is itself a constant expression;

-  Unary operators ``'+'``, ``'-'``, ``'~'``, and ``'!'``, but not ``'++'``
   or ``'--'`` (see :ref:`Unary Plus`, :ref:`Unary Minus`,
   :ref:`Prefix Increment`, and :ref:`Prefix Decrement`);

-  Casting conversions to numeric types (see :ref:`Cast Expression`);

-  Multiplicative operators ``'*'``, ``'/'``, and ``'%'`` (see
   :ref:`Multiplicative Expressions`);

-  Additive operators ``'+'`` and ``'-'`` (see :ref:`Additive Expressions`);

-  Shift operators ``'<<'``, ``'>>'``, and ``'>>>'`` (see
   :ref:`Shift Expressions`);

-  Relational operators ``'<'``, ``'<='``, ``'>'``, and ``'>='`` (see
   :ref:`Relational Expressions`);

-  Equality operators ``'=='`` and ``'!='`` (see :ref:`Equality Expressions`);

-  Bitwise and logical operators ``'&'``, ``'^'``, and ``'|'`` (see
   :ref:`Bitwise and Logical Expressions`);

-  Conditional-and operator ``'&&'`` (see :ref:`Conditional-And Expression`),
   and conditional-or operator ``'||'`` (see :ref:`Conditional-Or Expression`);

-  Ternary conditional operator ``condition?whenTrue:whenFalse``
   (see :ref:`Ternary Conditional Expressions`);

-  Parenthesized expressions (see :ref:`Parenthesized Expression`) that contain
   constant expressions.

212: Constant Or Variable Declarations
213: *********************************
214: 
215: .. meta:
216:     frontend_status: Done
217: 
218: *Constant or variable declarations* define new mutable or immutable variables within the
219: enclosing context.
220: 
221: ``Let`` and ``const`` declarations have the initialization part that presumes
222: execution, and actually act as statements.
223: 
224: .. index::
225:    variable declaration
226:    constant declaration
227:    let declaration
228:    const declaration
229: 
230: The syntax of a *constant or variable declaration* is presented below:
231: 
232: .. code-block:: abnf
233: 
234:     constantOrVariableDeclaration:
235:         annotationUsage?
236:         ( variableDeclaration
237:         | constantDeclaration
238:         )

--- 7_expressions.rst:4033-4044 ---
4033: The syntax of *cast expression* is as follows:
4034: 
4035: .. code-block:: abnf
4036: 
4037:     castExpression:
4038:         expression 'as' type
4039:         ;
4040: 
4041: *Cast expression* in the form ``expr as target`` applies the *cast operator*
4042: ``as`` to ``expr`` by issuing the value of a specified ``target`` type. Thus,
4043: the type of a cast expression is always the ``target`` type.
4044: 
--- 7_expressions.rst:4109-4147 ---
4109: ``expr as target`` expression:
4110: 
4111: -  ``expr`` is a numeric literal, see :ref:`Type Inference for Constant Expressions`
4112:    for detail;
4113: 
4114: -  ``expr`` is an :ref:`Array Literal`, and ``target`` is an *array type* or
4115:    a *tuple type* (see :ref:`Array Literal Type Inference from Context` for
4116:    detail);
4117: 
4118: -  ``expr`` is an :ref:`Object Literal`, and ``target`` is *class type*,
4119:    *interface type*, or :ref:`Record Utility Type` (see the subsections of
4120:    :ref:`Object Literal` for detail).
4121: 
4122: .. index::
4123:    cast expression
4124:    type inference
4125:    expression
4126:    numeric type
4127:    value
4128:    interface type
4129:    record type
4130:    utility type
4131:    class type
4132:    interface type
4133:    object literal
4134: 
4135: This kind of a *cast expression* results in inferring the target type for
4136: ``expr``. This expression never causes a :index:`runtime error`
4137: by itself. However, the evaluation of array literal elements or
4138: object literal properties can cause a :index:`runtime error`.
4139: 
4140: Casting for numeric literals is represented in the
4141: example below:
4142: 
4143: .. code-block:: typescript
4144:    :linenos:
4145: 
4146:    let x = 1 as byte // OK
4147:    let y = 128 as byte // Compile-time error
--- 7_expressions.rst:8419-8452 ---
8419: Constant Expressions
8420: ********************
8421: 
8422: .. meta:
8423:     frontend_status: Done
8424: 
8425: *Constant expressions* are expressions with values that can be evaluated at
8426: compile time. If the evaluation *completes abruptly*, then a
8427: :index:`compile-time error` occurs.
8428: 
8429: The syntax of *constant expression* is presented below:
8430: 
8431: .. code-block:: abnf
8432: 
8433:     constantExpression:
8434:         expression
8435:         ;
8436: 
8437: A *constant expression* can be either of a value type (see
8438: :ref:`Value Types`) or of type ``string``, while being composed only of the
8439: following:
8440: 
8441: -  Literals of a predefined value types, and literals of type ``string`` (see
8442:    :ref:`Literals`);
8443: 
8444: -  Simple names that refer to constants declared in a surrounding block,
8445:    function, method, or lambda body, if the initializer of the referenced
8446:    constant declaration is itself a constant expression;
8447: 
8448: -  Unary operators ``'+'``, ``'-'``, ``'~'``, and ``'!'``, but not ``'++'``
8449:    or ``'--'`` (see :ref:`Unary Plus`, :ref:`Unary Minus`,
8450:    :ref:`Prefix Increment`, and :ref:`Prefix Decrement`);
8451: 
8452: -  Casting conversions to numeric types (see :ref:`Cast Expression`);
--- 7_expressions.rst:8549-8555 ---
8549: If a constant expression consists of a single integer literal or
8550: a constant of an integer type, it is also converted to the same big integer type.
8551: 
8552: :ref:`Type Inference for Constant Expressions` is always used to infer the
8553: type of constant expression. In other words, *big integer type* is an
8554: internal compiler type and values of this type cannot occur during execution.
8555: 
--- 15_semantics.rst:1568-1630 ---
1568: Type Inference for Constant Expressions
1569: =======================================
1570: 
1571: .. meta:
1572:     frontend_status: Partly
1573: 
1574: The type of a constant expression (see :ref:`Constant Expressions`) is first
1575: inferred from the context, if the context allows.
1576: The following contexts allow inference:
1577: 
1578: - :ref:`Assignment-like Contexts`;
1579: - :ref:`Cast Expression` context;
1580: - :ref:`Numeric Operator Contexts`.
1581: 
1582: If context does not allow to to infer type, the *value default type* is set as follows:
1583: 
1584: - ``int`` for a constant expression of a *big integer type* 
1585:   (see :ref:`Specifics of Constant Expressions Evaluation`) if its value
1586:   can be represented by a 32-bit number;
1587: - ``long`` for a constant expression of a *big integer type* 
1588:   (see :ref:`Specifics of Constant Expressions Evaluation`) if its value
1589:   can be represented by a 64-bit number;
1590: - ``double`` or ``float`` for a floating-point constant expression 
1591:   (see :ref:`Specifics of Constant Expressions Evaluation`).
1592: 
1593: Type inference is used only where the *target type* is one of the following:
1594: 
1595: - Case 1: *Numeric type* (see :ref:`Numeric Types`); or
1596: - Case 2: Union type (see :ref:`Union Types`) containing at least one
1597:   *numeric type*.
1598: 
1599: **Case 1: Target type is a numeric type**
1600: 
1601: Where a *target type* is numeric, the type of a constant expression is inferred
1602: from the *target type* and the value of the const expression,
1603: if one of following conditions is met:
1604: 
1605: #. *Target type* is equal to or larger than the value default type; or
1606: 
1607: #. Value is an *integer value* that fitting into the range
1608:    of the *target type*.
1609: 
1610: .. note::
1611:    A *floating-point suffix* if present declares a ``floating-point literal``,
1612:    and no type inference occurs.
1613: 
1614: If none of the conditions above is met, then the *target type* is not a
1615: valid type for the constant expression, and a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.
1616: 
1617: Type inference for a numeric *target type* is represented in the examples below:
1618: 
1619: .. code-block-meta:
1620:    expect-cte:
1621: 
1622: .. code-block:: typescript
1623:    :linenos:
1624: 
1625:     let l: long = 1     // OK, target type is larger than literal default type
1626:     let b: byte = 127   // OK, integer value fits type 'byte'
1627:     let f: float = 123f // OK, target type is the same as literal default type
1628:     let g: double = 11  // OK, target type is larger than literal default type
1629: 
1630:     b = 63 + 64           // OK, integer value fits type 'byte'
--- 6_conversions.rst:50-143 ---
50:     frontend_status: Partly
51:     todo: Need to adapt es2panda implementation after assignment and call contexts are unified
52: 
53: *Assignment-like contexts* include the following:
54: 
55: - *Declaration contexts* that allow setting an initial value to a variable
56:   (see :ref:`Variable Declarations`), a constant (see
57:   :ref:`Constant Declarations`), or a field (see :ref:`Field Declarations`)
58:   with an explicit type annotation;
59: 
60: - *Assignment contexts* that allow assigning (see :ref:`Assignment`) an
61:   expression value to a variable;
62: 
63: - *Call contexts* that allow assigning an argument value to a corresponding
64:   formal parameter of a function, method, constructor or lambda call (see
65:   :ref:`Function Call Expression`, :ref:`Method Call Expression`,
66:   :ref:`Explicit Constructor Call`, and :ref:`New Expressions`);
67: 
68: - *Return contexts* (see :ref:`return Statements`) the allow specifying
69:   a resultant value of a function, method or lambda call;
70: 
71: - *Composite literal contexts* that allow setting an expression value to an
72:   array element (see :ref:`Array Literal Type Inference from Context`),
73:   a class, or an interface field (see :ref:`Object Literal`);
74: 
75: .. index::
76:    assignment
77:    assignment-like context

80:    variable declaration

102:    value
103:    variable
104:    constant
105:    composite literal context
106:    function
107:    method
108:    constructor
109:    expression value
110:    array element
111: 
112: The examples are presented below:
113: 
114: .. code-block:: typescript
115:    :linenos:
116: 
117:       // declaration contexts:
118:       let x: number = 1
119:       const str: string = "done"
120:       class C {
121:         f: string = "aa"
122:       }
123: 
124:       // assignment contexts:
125:       x = str.length
126:       new C().f = "bb"
127:       function foo<T1, T2> (p1: T1, p2: T2) {
128:         let t1: T1 = p1
129:         let t2: T2 = p2
130:       }
131: 
132:       // call contexts:
133:       function foo(s: string) {}
134:       foo("hello")
135: 
136:       // composite literal contexts:
137:       let a: number[] = [str.length, 11]
138: 
139: In all these cases, the expression type must be *assignable* to the *target
140: type* (see :ref:`Assignability`).
141: *Assignability* allows using of one of :ref:`Implicit Conversions`.
142: If there is no applicable conversion, then a :index:`compile-time error`
143: occurs.

--- 2_lexical.rst:641-656 ---
641: If context allows inferring type, then :ref:`Type Inference for Constant Expressions`
642: is used to determine the type of an integer literal. Otherwise, the type is
643: determined as follows:
644: 
645: - If the literal value can be represented by a non-negative 32-bit number,
646:   i.e., the value is in the range ``0..max(int)``, then the type is ``int``;
647: 
648: - If the literal value can be represented by a non-negative 64-bit number,
649:   i.e., the value is in the range ``0..max(long)``, then the type is ``long``;
650: 
651: - Otherwise, a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.
652:
